title: The Non-Commuting Graph Γ(G)
content: `nonCommGraph` defines the non-commuting graph Γ(G) as a Lean 4 `SimpleGraph`: two vertices g, h are adjacent iff they do not commute and are distinct. The three required fields are: `Adj` (the relation), `symm` (symmetry — uses `Commute.symm` to convert `¬Commute g h` to `¬Commute h g`), and `loopless` (irreflexivity — follows since `g ≠ g` is false). The `noncomputable` qualifier arises because decidability of `¬Commute g h` for a general `Group G` may require classical logic.
mathContext: $\Gamma(G)$ has vertex set $G$ with edge $\{g, h\}$ iff $gh \neq hg$ and $g \neq h$. This is an undirected simple graph (no self-loops, symmetric relation). The `SimpleGraph` type in Mathlib provides the complete graph theory library, including clique numbers, chromatic numbers, and graph homomorphisms, enabling Neumann's theorem (about $\omega(\Gamma(G))$) and Gustafson's bound (about density of $\Gamma(G)$) to be stated in a unified framework.

title: The 5/8 Theorem as an Open Formalization Goal
content: `five_eighths_theorem` formalizes Gustafson's 1973 result as a `Prop` statement: for non-abelian finite groups H, `commProb H ≤ 5/8`. It is defined as a `def`, not proved — this is an explicit open formalization target. The non-abelian hypothesis `¬(∃ inst : CommGroup H, True)` encodes 'H does not admit a commutative group structure' using Lean 4's typeclass machinery. Gustafson's original proof: if Pr(G) > 1/4 then G/Z(G) has order ≤ 4, forcing abelianness via the class equation — a contradiction.
mathContext: Gustafson (1973): For non-abelian finite $G$, $\text{Pr}(G) \leq 5/8$. The bound is tight: both $D_4$ (dihedral group of order 8) and $Q_8$ (quaternion group) achieve $\text{Pr}(G) = 5/8$ exactly. Proof sketch: $\text{Pr}(G) = k(G)/|G|$ where $k(G)$ is the number of conjugacy classes. If $G$ is non-abelian, $|G/Z(G)| \geq 4$, forcing $k(G) \leq 5|G|/8$ by the class equation combined with size constraints on conjugacy classes.

title: Commuting Probability is Strictly Positive
content: `commProb_pos'` wraps Mathlib's `commProb_pos G` to give `0 < commProb G` for any finite group G. The positivity is immediate: at minimum, every element commutes with itself, so the set of commuting pairs contains the diagonal {(g,g) : g ∈ G} of size |G|. Thus commProb G ≥ 1/|G| > 0. The local wrapper makes the bound available without using the Mathlib lemma name directly.
mathContext: $\text{Pr}(G) \geq |G|/|G|^2 = 1/|G| > 0$. For concrete groups: $\text{Pr}(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) = 1$ (abelian); $\text{Pr}(S_3) = 1/2$; $\text{Pr}(D_4) = \text{Pr}(Q_8) = 5/8$; $\text{Pr}(S_n) = k(S_n)/n! \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ where $k(S_n)$ is the partition function. As groups grow more non-abelian, the commuting probability decreases toward 0.

title: Commutativity Degree = 1 iff Abelian: Element-wise Form
content: `commProb_one_iff_abelian` proves `commProb G = 1 ↔ ∀ a b : G, Commute a b`. The proof rewrites via `commProb_eq_one_iff` (Mathlib uses `Std.Commutative (· * ·)`) and converts between the typeclass form and explicit quantifiers: forward direction applies `.comm a b`, backward direction wraps in the `Std.Commutative` constructor `⟨fun a b => h a b⟩`. The element-wise form is more useful for downstream `apply` and `rw` tactics than the typeclass formulation.
mathContext: $\text{Pr}(G) = 1 \iff |\{(g,h): gh = hg\}| = |G|^2 \iff$ every pair commutes $\iff G$ is abelian. Mathlib's `commProb_eq_one_iff` uses `Std.Commutative (· * ·)` which bundles commutativity as a structure. The unwrapped form `\forall a b, Commute a b` directly matches the hypothesis in theorems like `commProb_lt_one_of_noncomm` and makes the logical chain transparent.

title: Abelian Groups Have Commuting Probability 1
content: `commProb_abelian` shows that for a `CommGroup H`, `commProb H = 1`. The proof is a one-liner: rewrite by `commProb_eq_one_iff` and provide `⟨mul_comm⟩` as the `Std.Commutative` witness. This works because `CommGroup` carries `mul_comm : ∀ a b, a * b = b * a`, which is precisely the `Std.Commutative` instance. This demonstrates how Lean 4's typeclass hierarchy makes such proofs trivial once the right API is assembled.
mathContext: For commutative group $H$: $\text{Pr}(H) = |H|^2 / |H|^2 = 1$. The `CommGroup H` typeclass in Lean 4 extends `Group H` with the `mul_comm` field. The `Std.Commutative` structure wraps a function satisfying commutativity; `⟨mul_comm⟩` provides `Std.Commutative.comm := mul_comm`. Standard examples: $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, product groups $A \times B$ with $A, B$ abelian, additive groups.

title: Non-Commuting Pair Forces Probability Strictly Below 1
content: `commProb_lt_one_of_noncomm` proves: if `∃ a b : G, ¬Commute a b`, then `commProb G < 1`. The proof combines `commProb_le_one` (giving ≤ 1) with a contradiction argument: if commProb G = 1, then `commProb_one_iff_abelian.mp` gives `∀ a b, Commute a b`, contradicting the non-commuting witness. The strict inequality `< 1` follows from `lt_of_le_of_ne` applied after ruling out equality.
mathContext: $\text{Pr}(G) < 1 \iff G$ is non-abelian. Proof structure: Suppose $\text{Pr}(G) = 1$. Then $\forall a, b: Commute\ a\ b$ (by `commProb_one_iff_abelian`). But the hypothesis gives $a, b$ with $\neg Commute\ a\ b$ — contradiction. Hence $\text{Pr}(G) \neq 1$, and since $\text{Pr}(G) \leq 1$, we get $\text{Pr}(G) < 1$. This bridges the graph-theoretic fact (Γ(G) has an edge) to the measure-theoretic fact (density < 1).

title: Non-Commuting Density as Complement of Commuting Probability
content: `nonCommDensity G = 1 - commProb G` is the fraction of ordered pairs (g, h) with gh ≠ hg. The quantity lies in [0, 1): it is 0 for abelian groups. The 5/8 theorem (open formalization goal) would add: nonCommDensity ≤ 3/8 for non-abelian groups. It equals the edge density of Γ(G) interpreted over all ordered pairs.
mathContext: $\delta(G) = 1 - \text{Pr}(G)$. Known values: $D_4, Q_8$: $\text{Pr} = 5/8$, $\delta = 3/8$; $S_3$: $\text{Pr}(S_3) = 3/6 = 1/2$, $\delta(S_3) = 1/2$ (3 conjugacy classes, $|S_3| = 6$); $S_n$ ($n \geq 5$): $\text{Pr}(S_n) \to 0$, $\delta(S_n) \to 1$. The 5/8 theorem says no finite group has $\text{Pr}(G) \in (5/8, 1)$, i.e., $\delta(G) \in (0, 3/8)$.

title: Zero Density Characterizes Abelian Groups
content: `nonCommDensity_zero_iff_abelian` proves `nonCommDensity G = 0 ↔ ∀ a b, Commute a b`. Forward direction: `1 - commProb G = 0` implies `commProb G = 1` (by `linarith`), then `commProb_one_iff_abelian.mp`. Backward direction: every pair commutes implies `commProb G = 1` (by `commProb_one_iff_abelian.mpr`), then `linarith` gives `1 - 1 = 0`. The `linarith` tactic handles the rational arithmetic automatically.
mathContext: $\delta(G) = 0 \iff 1 - \text{Pr}(G) = 0 \iff \text{Pr}(G) = 1 \iff G$ is abelian. This creates a three-way equivalence: $G$ abelian $\iff \text{Pr}(G) = 1 \iff \delta(G) = 0 \iff$ Γ(G) has no edges. The `linarith` tactic handles `1 - x = 0 ↔ x = 1` over $\mathbb{Q}$ automatically, making the numerical steps trivial.

title: Positive Density iff Non-Abelian: Completing the Dichotomy
content: `nonCommDensity_pos_of_noncomm` proves that when non-commuting elements exist, the non-commuting density is strictly positive. The proof is two steps: `commProb_lt_one_of_noncomm h` gives `commProb G < 1`, then `linarith` converts this to `0 < 1 - commProb G = nonCommDensity G`. Together with `nonCommDensity_zero_iff_abelian`, this establishes the complete density dichotomy: `nonCommDensity G = 0 ↔ abelian` and `nonCommDensity G > 0 ↔ non-abelian`.
mathContext: Combined picture: $\delta(G) = 0 \iff G$ abelian; $\delta(G) > 0 \iff G$ non-abelian. The 5/8 theorem (open formalization goal) would add: $\delta(G) \leq 3/8$ always, with equality for $D_4$ and $Q_8$. The Neumann connection (Erdős #1098): $\omega(\Gamma(G)) < \infty \iff [G:Z(G)] < \infty$ — a structural characterization via the clique number. Gustafson's theorem gives a density characterization. These are complementary: Neumann controls the maximum 'local concentration' of non-commutativity; Gustafson controls the 'global average'.
prerequisites: linarith for strict inequalities in ℚ
